title: The Great Sandstorm
summary: A class of students on a desert field trip is caught in a sudden sandstorm and must use their safety training to find shelter and stay calm until help arrives.
poll: In an emergency, staying calm matters more than anything else you can do.

versions.title: Caught in the Sandstorm
versions.text:
Omar's class goes on a trip. They go to see old desert plants. Ms. Huda is the teacher.

The bus stops near some hills. The class walks out. Omar and Lina walk near the front. The sky is blue and clear.

Then the wind picks up. The sky turns brown. Sand blows hard and fast. It is a big sandstorm!

The class can not see far. Sand stings their eyes. Some kids feel scared. They start to run.

Ms. Huda calls out loud. "Stop! Stay calm!" Omar thinks fast. He remembers his safety drill.

"Cover your mouth!" Omar says. He uses his scarf. Lina does it too. The class holds hands.

They find a big rock wall. It is good shelter from the wind. The class sits down low. They wait there together.

The wind howls outside. The class stays calm. They sing a soft song. It helps them wait.

At last, the wind stops. The sky turns blue again. A rescue truck comes. Everyone is safe.

Ms. Huda smiles at the class. "You did it," she says. "Your training kept you safe."

versions.text:
Omar's class goes on a field trip to see old desert plants. Their teacher, Ms. Huda, leads the way.

The bus stops near some rocky hills, and the class walks out into the open desert. Omar and Lina walk near the front. The sky above them is blue and clear.

Then, all at once, the wind picks up. The sky quickly turns brown and dusty, and sand blows hard and fast through the air. It is a big, sudden sandstorm!

The class can not see very far. Sand stings their eyes and faces. Some kids feel scared and start to run.

Ms. Huda calls out loudly to the class. "Stop! Stay calm, everyone!" Omar thinks fast and remembers his safety drill from school.

"Cover your mouth and nose!" Omar shouts. He uses his own scarf to cover his face. Lina does the same thing too. The whole class holds hands tightly.

They spot a big rock wall nearby. It blocks most of the wind. The class sits down low beside it, waiting together, close and quiet.

The wind howls outside their shelter. The class stays as calm as they can. They sing a soft, slow song together, and it helps them wait out the storm.

At last, the wind slows and stops. The brown sky slowly turns blue again. A rescue truck comes down the road. Everyone in the class is safe. Ms. Huda smiles warmly. "You did it," she says. "Your training kept you safe."

versions.title: The Great Sandstorm
versions.text:
Omar's class was heading out on a field trip to study old desert plants. Their teacher, Ms. Huda, led the way through the dry, rocky hills near their school.

The bus stopped near some rocky hills, and the class climbed out into the open desert. Omar and Lina walked near the front, pointing out small lizards between the stones. The sky above them was a bright, clear blue.

Then, without any warning, the wind picked up. The sky quickly turned a dusty brown, and sand began blowing hard through the air in every direction. Visibility dropped almost instantly, and a sandstorm had arrived.

The students could barely see a few steps ahead, and stinging sand blew into their eyes and faces. A wave of panic spread through the group, and several children started to run, unsure of where to go.

Ms. Huda shouted firmly over the roaring wind. "Stop! Everyone, remain together and stay calm!" Omar forced himself to think clearly, remembering the safety drill his school had practiced before.

"Cover your mouth and nose with cloth!" Omar called out. He pulled his scarf up over his face, and Lina quickly copied him. The rest of the class followed, holding hands tightly so nobody wandered off alone.

Together, they spotted a long rock wall that offered real shelter from the howling wind. The class crouched down low beside it, staying close together while they waited out the emergency.

The wind roared outside their shelter for what felt like a long time, but the class worked hard to stay calm. They sang a slow, quiet song together, which helped take their mind off their fear.

Eventually, the wind weakened and finally died down. The brown sky slowly cleared back to blue, and a rescue truck arrived along the dusty road. Everyone was safe. Ms. Huda praised the students, reminding them that their calm thinking and practiced training had kept them safe during the emergency.

versions.title: The Great Sandstorm
versions.text:
Omar's classmates were traveling on an educational field trip to investigate ancient desert vegetation, and their teacher, Ms. Huda, guided the group through the arid, rocky hills near their school, meticulously explaining the names and traditional uses of each plant as they proceeded.

The bus stopped near a cluster of rocky hills, and the students climbed out into the open desert, chatting cheerfully among themselves. Omar and Lina walked near the front of the group, pointing out small lizards darting between the sunlit stones. The sky overhead remained a brilliant, cloudless blue, giving no hint of what was about to happen.

Then, with no meteorological warning whatsoever, the wind abruptly intensified. The sky rapidly transformed into a swirling wall of dusty brown, and sand began hurtling through the air in every direction. Visibility collapsed almost instantly, and the class realized, with mounting alarm, that a genuine sandstorm had struck without warning.

The students could barely distinguish shapes more than a few steps ahead, and stinging sand lashed directly at their eyes and faces. A wave of panic rippled through the group, and several children bolted in different directions, uncertain of where safety might even lie.

Ms. Huda shouted firmly over the howling wind, projecting her voice with practiced composure. "Stop! Everyone, remain together and stay calm!" Omar forced himself to think clearly, drawing on the safety precautions his school had rehearsed many times before this frightening moment.

"Cover your mouth and nose with cloth!" Omar called out, raising his voice above the roaring wind. He pulled his scarf firmly over his face, and Lina immediately copied him. The rest of the class followed suit, coordinating their movements and holding hands tightly so nobody would wander off alone.

Together, the group spotted a long rock wall that offered genuine shelter from the howling gale. The class crouched low beside it, maintaining close contact with one another while they waited out the emergency with remarkable resilience.

The wind roared outside their shelter for what felt like an eternity, yet the class worked hard to preserve its composure throughout the ordeal. They sang a slow, quiet song together, a simple act that helped distract everyone from mounting fear and uncertainty.

Eventually, the wind weakened and finally subsided completely. The brown sky gradually cleared back to blue, and a rescue truck arrived along the dusty road, its crew having coordinated quickly once reports of the storm reached them. Everyone in the class emerged safe and unharmed. Ms. Huda praised the students warmly, reminding them that their composure and practiced training had truly kept them safe during a genuinely dangerous emergency.

Stinging particles of abrasive sand lashed relentlessly at their eyes and faces, nearly obscuring their vision entirely, and a wave of uncontrollable panic rippled through the group as several children bolted impulsively in different directions, uncertain of where safety might even be located amid the surrounding chaos.

Ms. Huda shouted firmly over the howling wind, projecting her voice with practiced composure despite her own underlying concern, and Omar forced himself to concentrate clearly, deliberately drawing on the safety precautions his school had rehearsed repeatedly before this frightening moment arrived unexpectedly.

Calling out instructions above the roaring wind, Omar pulled his scarf firmly over his face and urged his classmates to cover their mouths and noses with cloth; Lina immediately replicated his actions, and the remainder of the class followed suit, coordinating their movements carefully while holding hands tightly so that nobody would wander off alone into the swirling, disorienting sand.

Together, the group identified a long rock wall offering genuine protective shelter from the relentless gale, and they crouched low beside it, maintaining close physical contact with one another while enduring the emergency with remarkable resilience, singing a slow, quiet song that helped distract everyone from their mounting fear and uncertainty about when the storm might finally subside.

Eventually, the wind gradually weakened and subsided completely, the brown sky cleared back to blue, and a rescue truck arrived along the dusty road, its crew having coordinated efficiently once reports of the storm reached them from a nearby village, leaving everyone in the class safe and completely unharmed.

Ms. Huda praised the students warmly afterward, reminding them that their composure and diligently practiced training, rather than mere luck, had genuinely determined the outcome of an authentically dangerous emergency, a lesson she hoped they would remember long after the sand had finally settled.

keyWords.definition: a strong wind that blows a lot of sand through the air
keyWords.example: The hikers had to stop walking when a sandstorm blew across the trail.

keyWords.definition: a long piece of cloth worn around the neck or face
keyWords.example: She wrapped her scarf around her face to keep out the dust.

keyWords.definition: a place that protects you from danger or bad weather
keyWords.example: The hikers found shelter under a big tree during the rain.

keyWords.definition: quiet and not worried or upset
keyWords.example: The nurse spoke in a calm voice to help the child feel better.

keyWords.definition: being free from danger or harm
keyWords.example: Wearing a helmet is an easy way to add safety when you ride a bike.

questions.stem: What is this story mostly about?
options: A class that gets caught in a sandstorm and stays calm to find shelter together
A class trip to the beach that gets rained on, so the children go home early
A bus that breaks down somewhere in the desert, and the driver must call for help
A teacher who forgets the way back home, so the class walks in circles all day
questions.why: The story follows Omar's class as a sandstorm hits, and they stay calm, use their safety training, and find shelter until help comes.

wrong.B: The class trip is in the desert, not at the beach, and there is no rain.
wrong.C: The bus does not break down in the story.
wrong.D: The teacher does not get lost; she leads the class to safety.

questions.stem: What did Omar tell his classmates to do first?
options: Run as fast as they possibly could away from the storm
Cover their mouth and nose with cloth
Dig a deep hole in the sand to hide
Call their parents right away on the phone
questions.why: Omar calls out for everyone to cover their mouth and nose with cloth, like a scarf, to protect themselves from the blowing sand.

wrong.A: Running could make things worse; the class stays together instead.
wrong.C: The story does not say anyone digs a hole.
wrong.D: No one calls their parents on a phone in the story.

questions.stem: Where did the class find shelter from the storm?
options: Inside a dark cave full of bats
Under the broken school bus
Behind a big rock wall
Inside a small nearby shop
questions.why: The class finds a big rock wall that blocks the wind and sits down low behind it to wait out the storm.

wrong.A: There is no cave with bats in the story.
wrong.B: The bus is not broken, and the class does not hide under it.
wrong.D: There is no shop near them in the desert.

questions.stem: In the story, the word shelter means —
options: a place that is open to the wind and sand
a kind of loud, scary sound
a type of school bus used for trips
a place that protects you from danger
questions.why: The rock wall acts as a shelter because it blocks the wind and keeps the class safer from the storm.

wrong.A: A shelter protects you; it is not left open to danger.
wrong.B: Shelter is not a sound.
wrong.C: Shelter is not a kind of bus.

questions.stem: What happened right after the wind picked up?
options: The sky turned brown and sand began to blow hard
The rescue truck arrived to help everyone
The class sang a quiet song together
Ms. Huda praised the students for staying calm
questions.why: As soon as the wind picked up, the sky turned brown and sand began blowing hard through the air.

wrong.B: The rescue truck comes much later, after the storm.
wrong.C: The singing happens while they wait behind the rock wall, later on.
wrong.D: Ms. Huda's praise comes at the very end of the story.

questions.stem: Why did some kids start to run when the sandstorm hit?
options: They were playing a fun game in the sand
They felt scared and did not know what to do
They were excited to see the big storm
Ms. Huda told every student to run
questions.why: The sudden storm scared the children, and in their fear some of them started running without a plan.

wrong.A: This is not a game; the storm is a real danger.
wrong.C: The story shows fear, not excitement, in the children.
wrong.D: Ms. Huda actually tells everyone to stop and stay calm.

questions.stem: How did Omar feel when he remembered his safety drill?
options: Confused and too sleepy to move or speak
Angry at all of his classmates in the bus
Focused and ready to help his classmates
Bored with the whole class trip to the park
questions.why: Omar thinks fast and quickly tells his classmates what to do, showing that he feels focused and ready to help.

wrong.A: Omar is alert, not confused or sleepy.
wrong.B: The story does not show Omar getting angry at anyone.
wrong.D: Omar is actively helping, not bored.

questions.stem: Why does the story end with Ms. Huda saying the training kept them safe?
options: To show that teachers are always right about everything they say
To explain how to drive a rescue truck in a sandstorm
To show that sandstorms are never dangerous for children outdoors
To show that practicing safety steps really helps in an emergency
questions.why: The ending shows that because the class had practiced the safety drill, they knew what to do and stayed safe.

wrong.A: The story is not about whether teachers are always right.
wrong.B: The story does not explain how to drive a truck.
wrong.C: The sandstorm is shown as dangerous, which is why safety steps mattered.

LOW.prompt: Do you think the class's safety training helped them during the sandstorm? Explain why or why not, using at least two facts from the story.
checklist: I clearly said what I think.
I used at least two facts from the story.
I wrote complete sentences with capital letters and periods.
LOW.modelAnswer: I think the safety training helped the class a lot. Omar remembered to tell everyone to cover their mouth and nose with a scarf, which kept the blowing sand out. The class also found shelter behind a big rock wall and stayed calm until the storm passed. Because of their training, everyone in the class was safe when the rescue truck finally arrived.

keyWords.definition: to stay in a place or in a certain condition
keyWords.example: The hikers decided to remain near the shelter until the rain stopped.

keyWords.definition: a sudden, strong feeling of fear that makes people act without thinking
keyWords.example: A moment of panic spread through the crowd when the lights went out.

keyWords.definition: how far or how clearly you can see
keyWords.example: Thick fog reduced visibility on the highway that morning.

keyWords.definition: a sudden, serious situation that needs quick action
keyWords.example: The lifeguard was trained to handle any emergency at the pool.

keyWords.definition: practice of the exact steps to follow in an emergency
keyWords.example: Every month, the school holds a fire drill so students know what to do.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the central idea of the story?
options: A group of students get lost forever in the desert and are never found by any rescue team or by their families.
A class caught in a sudden sandstorm works together, remembers safety training, and finds shelter until help arrives.
A teacher argues with her students about where to go during a long field trip, and they split into two groups.
A bus breaks down on a lonely road and nobody knows what to do, so they all wait in the hot sun for a day.
questions.why: The story centers on the class facing a sudden sandstorm and using teamwork and their practiced drill to reach safety.

wrong.A: The students are rescued, not lost forever.
wrong.C: Ms. Huda does not argue with the students; she calmly leads them.
wrong.D: The bus is never mentioned as broken down.

questions.stem: What safety steps did Omar remind his classmates to follow?
options: Cover their mouths and noses and hold hands together
Run in every possible direction to try to find help on their own
Climb to the top of the rocky hills
Call out for their parents loudly
questions.why: Omar tells everyone to cover their mouth and nose with cloth and to hold hands so nobody wanders off.

wrong.B: Running in different directions is what the panicked students do before Omar's instructions.
wrong.C: The story does not mention climbing the hills during the storm.
wrong.D: The story never shows students calling for their parents.

questions.stem: What did the class do while waiting out the storm behind the rock wall?
options: They argued about whose fault the storm was
They tried to walk back to the bus
They fell asleep until the storm ended
They sang a quiet song together to stay calm
questions.why: While sheltering behind the rock wall, the class sings a slow, quiet song together to help them stay calm.

wrong.A: The story shows no arguing among the students.
wrong.B: Walking back to the bus during the storm would be unsafe, and the class does not attempt this.
wrong.C: The class stays alert and calm, not asleep.

questions.stem: In the story, the word visibility means —
options: how loud a sound is
how fast the wind blows
how far or clearly you can see
how many students are in the class
questions.why: When visibility drops, the students can barely see ahead of them because of the blowing sand.

wrong.A: Visibility is about sight, not sound.
wrong.B: Visibility describes sight, not wind speed.
wrong.D: Visibility has nothing to do with counting students.

questions.stem: Why did panic spread through the group when the sandstorm began?
options: The students could barely see and did not know where to go
The bus had already left without them, and they were far from home
Ms. Huda had disappeared, and nobody could find her
The lizards they saw earlier scared them, so they ran in all directions
questions.why: With visibility dropping and sand stinging their faces, the students did not know where it was safe to go, which caused panic.

wrong.B: The bus is not mentioned as leaving.
wrong.C: Ms. Huda stays with the class the whole time and calls out to them.
wrong.D: The lizards appear earlier and are not connected to the panic.

questions.stem: What does Omar's quick thinking during the storm suggest about his character?
options: He panics easily under pressure
He prefers to work alone rather than with others
He is not very concerned about his classmates
He remembers and applies what he has practiced
questions.why: Omar recalls his safety drill and immediately shares it with his classmates, showing he remembers and applies his training under pressure.

wrong.A: Omar stays level-headed rather than panicking.
wrong.B: Omar works to keep the whole class together, not alone.
wrong.C: Omar's actions show real concern for his classmates' safety.

questions.stem: Why did Ms. Huda project her voice with composure despite her own concern?
options: She was not actually worried at all, and she wanted to joke with them
She wanted to calm the students and help them think clearly
She wanted the class to stop singing so the room would be quiet
She wanted to scold the students for running in the hallway
questions.why: By staying outwardly calm while shouting instructions, Ms. Huda helps the frightened students focus and listen.

wrong.A: The story says she has underlying concern, so she is worried.
wrong.C: The singing happens later and helps the class, which she does not stop.
wrong.D: Ms. Huda calls out to help, not to scold anyone.

questions.stem: How does the author organize the events of the story?
options: By comparing two different storms that hit the coast in two different years of the past
By describing Ms. Huda's entire teaching career, from her first class to her retirement day
By following the class from the calm start of the trip through the emergency to final safety
By listing facts about desert lizards and the places where each kind of lizard lives
questions.why: The story moves in order from the calm beginning of the field trip, through the sudden sandstorm, to the class finally reaching safety.

wrong.A: Only one storm is described in the story.
wrong.B: The story focuses on one field trip, not her whole career.
wrong.D: The lizards are a small detail, not the organizing structure.

MID.prompt: Explain how the class worked together to stay safe during the sandstorm. Use at least two details from the story.
checklist: I explained how the class worked together clearly.
I used at least two details from the story.
I organized my ideas in a clear order.
MID.modelAnswer: The class worked together by following Omar's quick instructions during the emergency. He reminded everyone to cover their mouths and noses with cloth and to hold hands so nobody would wander off alone. Once they found shelter behind a rock wall, the class sang a quiet song together, which helped everyone remain calm until the rescue truck finally arrived.

keyWords.definition: a calm, controlled state of mind, especially under pressure
keyWords.example: The pilot kept her composure even when the engine made a strange noise.

keyWords.definition: to organize different people or actions so they work well together
keyWords.example: The event planners had to coordinate dozens of volunteers for the festival.

keyWords.definition: relating to the weather and the science that studies it
keyWords.example: The farmers checked the meteorological report before planting their crops.

keyWords.definition: an action taken in advance to prevent harm or danger
keyWords.example: As a precaution, the school keeps extra water in every classroom.

keyWords.definition: the ability to recover from or handle difficulty calmly
keyWords.example: The team showed real resilience after losing the first two games of the season.

questions.stem: Which statement best captures the central idea of the story?
options: A field trip turns into a genuine emergency, and the students' composure and rehearsed precautions, rather than luck, determine their safe outcome.
A field trip ends early because of bad weather reports, and the bus drives home before lunch time, with all students tired and sad.
A class learns which desert plants are best to eat during emergencies and gathers them all day, when the teacher is not looking.
A teacher punishes students for running during the storm, so they feel afraid of the whole trip and refuse to go on any more field trips.
questions.why: The story's resolution emphasizes that the students' composure and their rehearsed safety precautions, not chance, led to their safe outcome.

wrong.B: The trip is cut short by the storm itself, not by an early weather report.
wrong.C: The story focuses on plant names earlier, not survival food.
wrong.D: Ms. Huda calls the students back to safety; she does not punish them.

questions.stem: According to the story, what triggered the sudden drop in visibility?
options: A dust cloud created by passing vehicles
Sand hurtling through the air in every direction once the wind intensified
Smoke from a nearby fire
Fog rolling in slowly from the coast after a sudden drop in temperature overnight
questions.why: The story explains that once the wind abruptly intensified, sand hurtled through the air in every direction, causing visibility to collapse.

wrong.A: No vehicles are mentioned causing dust.
wrong.C: There is no fire or smoke in the story.
wrong.D: The desert setting rules out coastal fog.

questions.stem: What specific action did the rescue crew take once they learned of the storm?
options: They waited at the school until the storm passed over the town
They ignored the reports entirely and stayed home
They coordinated quickly and arrived once the storm subsided
They sent a helicopter instead of a truck to the village
questions.why: In the story, the rescue crew coordinated efficiently once reports of the storm reached them, and their truck arrived after the wind weakened.

wrong.A: The crew travels to the class rather than waiting at the school.
wrong.B: The crew responds quickly rather than ignoring the reports.
wrong.D: A truck arrives, not a helicopter.

questions.stem: In the story, composure most nearly means —
options: a sudden, overwhelming burst of fear or panic that spreads quickly through a group
a type of desert plant
a loud warning siren
a state of calm, controlled behavior under pressure
questions.why: Ms. Huda and the class work to preserve their composure, meaning they stay calm and controlled even while frightened.

wrong.A: Composure is the opposite of panic.
wrong.B: Composure is not a plant.
wrong.C: Composure is not a siren or sound.

questions.stem: What was the main effect of Omar's clear thinking during the emergency?
options: The students took protective action together instead of scattering
The storm ended more quickly than anyone expected, so the class went home
The class panicked even more than they did before, and ran away
Ms. Huda no longer needed to give any instructions to the class at all
questions.why: Because Omar thought clearly and gave instructions, the class covered their faces, held hands, and moved to shelter together instead of scattering.

wrong.B: Nothing in the story connects Omar's actions to the storm's length.
wrong.C: Omar's actions reduce panic rather than increase it.
wrong.D: Ms. Huda continues to lead and encourage the class throughout.

questions.stem: What can readers infer about why Ms. Huda's warning had such an immediate effect on the class?
options: The students were already planning to stop running on their own before she even spoke
Her firm, practiced tone conveyed authority the frightened students could trust
The wind had already stopped by the time she shouted
The students could not actually hear her over the wind
questions.why: Ms. Huda shouts with practiced composure, and her firm, confident tone helps the frightened students trust her and listen.

wrong.A: The students are running in panic, not already planning to stop.
wrong.C: The wind is still roaring when she shouts.
wrong.D: The students respond to her words, showing they heard her.

questions.stem: How does Omar's response to the crisis differ from the panicked students' initial reactions?
options: Omar also runs blindly, just in a different direction, and he gets lost in the smoke
Omar relies entirely on Ms. Huda and takes no independent action, even when she is far away
Omar draws on rehearsed precautions to act deliberately, while the panicked students react impulsively
Omar and the panicked students behave in exactly the same way, shouting and pushing at the door
questions.why: While some students bolt impulsively out of fear, Omar deliberately applies precautions from his safety drill, showing a clear contrast in their reactions.

wrong.A: Omar does not run; he stops to think and act with purpose.
wrong.B: Omar takes his own initiative by calling out instructions before Ms. Huda finishes speaking.
wrong.D: Their behavior is clearly different, not identical.

questions.stem: Why does the author conclude the story with Ms. Huda's remark that training, rather than luck, determined the outcome?
options: To suggest that luck, rather than any preparation at all, is actually what mattered most that day
To criticize Omar for acting without permission
To argue that field trips should be canceled permanently
To emphasize that preparation and composure, not chance, kept the students safe
questions.why: The closing line reinforces the story's message that rehearsed precautions and calm thinking, not random chance, are what kept the class safe.

wrong.A: The ending explicitly credits training over luck.
wrong.B: Ms. Huda praises Omar; she does not criticize him.
wrong.C: The story never suggests ending field trips.

HIGH.prompt: The poll says staying calm matters more in an emergency than anything else you can do. Do you agree or disagree? Support your argument with evidence from the story about precautions, composure, and teamwork.
checklist: I stated a clear position on the poll statement.
I supported my position with specific evidence from the story.
I addressed at least one point someone might make against my view.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I partly agree that staying calm matters most, but the story shows that calm alone was not enough without rehearsed precautions to act on. Omar's composure let him think clearly, but it was his memory of the safety drill, covering faces and holding hands, that actually protected the class from the blowing sand. Ms. Huda's own composure also mattered because her firm, practiced tone helped frightened students trust her and stop running. Someone might argue that quick action matters more than calm itself, but without composure the class could not have coordinated their actions at all, so both qualities worked together to keep everyone safe.

LOW.stem: Why does Omar's class go on the trip?
options: To see old desert plants
To swim in a lake
To meet a rescue crew
To sing a song
LOW.why: In the text, the class goes to see old desert plants.

wrong.B: No lake is in the story.
wrong.C: The rescue truck comes later.
wrong.D: They sing during the storm, not for the trip.

LOW.stem: Why can the class not see far in the storm?
options: The sun is very bright
Sand blows hard and fast
They wear heavy scarves
The hills are too high
LOW.why: The text says sand blows hard and fast, so the class cannot see far.

wrong.A: The sky turns brown, not bright.
wrong.C: Scarves come later, to cover their mouths.
wrong.D: The hills are not the reason.

LOW.stem: Why does the class hold hands?
options: To keep warm
To play a game
To stay together
To dance
LOW.why: In a strong storm they cannot see far, so holding hands keeps everyone together.

wrong.A: The text does not say they are cold.
wrong.B: This is an emergency, not a game.
wrong.D: They sing, but they do not dance.

LOW.stem: The text says Omar used his scarf. What is a scarf?
options: a cloth to cover your face or neck
a tool used to dig in the sand
a truck that comes to help people
a song to sing when scared
LOW.why: Omar used his scarf to cover his face in the sandstorm, so a scarf is a cloth for the face or neck.

wrong.B: A scarf is not a tool for digging.
wrong.C: The rescue truck is different.
wrong.D: The class sang a song, but that is not a scarf.

MID.stem: What are Omar and Lina doing before the storm?
options: Pointing out small lizards
Running back to the bus
Singing a quiet slow song
Covering their faces up
MID.why: The story says they walked near the front, pointing out small lizards.

wrong.B: They only run after the storm starts.
wrong.C: The class sings during the storm.
wrong.D: They cover their faces after the storm hits.

MID.stem: Why does the class hold hands tightly?
options: To keep warm in the wind
So nobody wanders off alone
To walk faster to the bus
To show they are brave
MID.why: In the story, they held hands tightly so nobody wandered off alone.

wrong.A: Warmth is not mentioned.
wrong.C: They stay together and do not hurry to the bus.
wrong.D: Bravery is not given as the reason.

MID.stem: In the story, the word crouched means the class —
options: ran far away
stood up tall
bent down low
looked at plants
MID.why: They crouched down low beside the wall to stay out of the wind.

wrong.A: They stayed beside the wall.
wrong.B: Crouched is the opposite of standing tall.
wrong.D: They were waiting out the storm.

MID.stem: Why does the author describe the sky as bright, clear blue at the start?
options: To show the storm is coming from far
To list the plants on the hill
To contrast with the sudden storm
To tell what time it is
MID.why: The clear blue sky makes the sudden brown storm feel like a big surprise.

wrong.A: The storm comes without warning.
wrong.B: The sky is not about plants.
wrong.D: The sky is not used to tell time.

HIGH.stem: What was Ms. Huda doing as she guided the group?
options: Teaching the names and uses of plants
Watching for a rescue crew
Counting the lizards on the stones
Planning a long bus ride
HIGH.why: In the story, she explained the names and traditional uses of each plant.

wrong.B: The rescue crew comes at the end.
wrong.C: The students point out lizards, not Ms. Huda.
wrong.D: The bus stopped near the hills.

HIGH.stem: In the story, the word bolted most nearly means —
options: ran off suddenly
sat down slowly
stopped to listen
held hands
HIGH.why: Several children bolted in different directions in panic, so it means ran off suddenly.

wrong.B: The children panicked and did not sit.
wrong.C: They ran instead of listening.
wrong.D: They held hands later, after Omar's call.

HIGH.stem: Why did singing a quiet song help the class?
options: It scared the sand away
It called the rescue truck
It showed them where to go
It distracted them from fear
HIGH.why: The story says the song helped distract everyone from mounting fear.

wrong.A: A song cannot move the sand.
wrong.B: The crew came because of reports of the storm.
wrong.C: They were already at the rock wall.

HIGH.stem: Why does the author describe the sky as clear and cloudless just before the storm?
options: To show the storm was unexpected
To say the day was too hot
To explain why the bus stopped
To warn that rain was near
HIGH.why: The phrase shows the sandstorm struck with no warning signs.

wrong.B: The heat is not the point of the phrase.
wrong.C: The bus stops near the hills for the trip.
wrong.D: The storm brings sand, not rain.
